---
title: Architecture
description: How Flux works — the parse → typecheck → lower → diff → patch → VM pipeline, the 16 crates, stable node identity, and the three normative contracts.
type: explanation
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

import { Aside, Code, FileTree } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux is a Rust workspace of 16 crates (~63k lines) plus native host
implementations in Swift and Kotlin. Understanding the pipeline explains
every observable behavior — why saves are fast, why state survives edits,
and why dev and release stay equivalent.

## The pipeline

<Code lang="text" code={` main.flux
     │
     ▼
┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐
│ flux-parser │──▶│ flux-types  │──▶│       flux-ir        │
│ (lex/parse) │   │ (typecheck) │   │ (Reactive Tree IR)   │
└─────────────┘   └─────────────┘   └──────────┬───────────┘
                                               │
                    ┌──────────────────────────┴──────────────┐
                    ▼ dev                                     ▼ release
        ┌──────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │ flux-differ  │──▶│ flux-ir-serde │      │    flux-codegen-core    │
        │ (tree diff)  │   │ (MsgPack patch│      │ (data-driven emitter)   │
        └──────────────┘   └───────┬───────┘      └───────────┬─────────────┘
                                   │ WebSocket :7331           │
                                   ▼                           ├─▶ flux-codegen-swift  → SwiftUI
                        ┌──────────────────┐                   └─▶ flux-codegen-kotlin → Compose
                        │  Host app VM +   │
                        │  signal graph +  │   ◀── validated against
                        │  shadow tree     │        92 golden ISA vectors
                        │ (Swift / Kotlin) │        (tests/isa-vectors/)
                        └──────────────────┘`} />

One source, two consumers. The dev tier diffs and patches; the release tier
codegens. Both start from the same Reactive Tree IR, which is what the
parity harness verifies.

## The crates

| Crate | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `flux-syntax` | Spans, NodeId, FNV-1a node-id hashing, value/patch vocabulary |
| `flux-parser` | Hand-written lexer + recursive-descent parser with error recovery |
| `flux-types` | Type checker over the parse tree |
| `flux-ir` | Reactive Tree IR: arena, stable u32 node IDs, ClosureIR bytecode table, InstanceRegistry |
| `flux-ir-serde` | Binary patch (de)serialization — MessagePack, blake3 content addressing |
| `flux-differ` | Structural tree differ producing minimal edit scripts |
| `flux-vm-ref` | Reference register VM — the behavioral oracle for the ISA |
| `flux-devserver` | Hot-reload pipeline, WebSocket patch channel, HTTP asset server |
| `flux-codegen-core` | Shared data-driven emitter (Backend trait, primitive registry) |
| `flux-codegen-swift` | SwiftUI backend with a node-ID bridge |
| `flux-codegen-kotlin` | Jetpack Compose backend with a node-ID bridge |
| `flux-cli` | The `flux` binary |
| `flux-parity` | Dev VM == release codegen parity harness |
| `flux-lsp` | Language server (async-lsp) |
| `flux-devtools-ui` | gpui DevTools desktop app over the same wire protocol |
| `flux-perf-harness` | Render-performance measurement against the latency budgets |

## Stable node identity

Node IDs are stable, content-derived **FNV-1a-32 hashes — never sequential**.
Two tag families keep expression and declaration IDs disjoint, and the
codegen backends thread the exact same family tags through their node-ID
bridges.

This is the load-bearing trick behind hot reload: because IDs are stable
across edits where structure does not change, a hot swap preserves component
state. The todo app's half-typed text field survives every save because the
host matches the new tree against the old one by ID.

## Prop indexing

Prop indices are FNV-1a-32 of the prop **name**, masked to `u16`, derived
identically by the host kits (`PropsIndex.propIndexForName` on Android).
Indices are never hardcoded — a hardcoded index desyncs from the server and
renders silently blank UI.

## The shadow tree and keyed reconciliation

The shadow tree is not a tree of raw native views. Each `ShadowNode` holds
its materialized props in a platform-observable store: on Android, props
live in a Compose `MutableState` (injected via `propsStateFactory`, because
a plain `var` is invisible to snapshot tracking); on iOS the tree is
observed natively.

**Keyed reconciliation** matches children by `nodeId` — an existing node is
reordered, never recreated — preserving scroll position, text field
contents, and screen state across diffs and router push/pop.

## Three normative contracts

<Aside type="caution">Three contracts are normative and versioned in
`docs/spec/mlp-appendices.md`: the **wire protocol** (Appendix D), the **VM
ISA** (Appendix E), and the **adapter contracts** (Appendix F). Cross-cutting
changes to any of them require an ADR and a protocol version bump.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Reactivity](/explanation/reactivity/) — the invariant that makes a tap
  cost one update.
- [Dev vs release](/explanation/dev-vs-release/) — why two execution tiers.


---

---
title: Dev vs release
description: Why Flux has two execution tiers over one IR — interpreted patches for liveness in dev, native codegen for zero runtime overhead in release — and how parity is proven.
type: explanation
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

import { Card, CardGrid, Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux has two execution modes. Both consume the **same Reactive Tree IR**
produced by the lowering pass — they differ only in how the host turns that
IR into pixels.

## Dev mode — interpreted and patched

In dev, a precompiled **host app** ships to the device. The dev server
parses `.flux`, lowers it to the Reactive Tree IR, diffs it against the
previous tree, and ships **binary patches** over a WebSocket. The host's
embedded register-based bytecode VM and signal graph apply the patch and
mutate a shadow tree of native views.

- Fast iteration: save → diff → patch, with no app recompile.
- Full introspection: the wire frame, the VM outcome, and the reconcile
  trace are all observable.
- The `trace` sink is free in production (ADR-0027 INV-2): no overhead when
  no driver is attached.

## Release mode — codegen'd native

In release, the same IR is **codegen'd** to idiomatic Swift/SwiftUI and
Kotlin/Jetpack Compose. There is no VM, no patch protocol, no shadow tree —
the output is a normal native app.

<CardGrid>
  <Card title="SwiftUI" icon="seti:swift">
    `compo Counter` → `struct Counter: View`. `state` → `@State`.
    `Column(gap:)` → `VStack(spacing:)`.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Jetpack Compose" icon="seti:kotlin">
    `compo Counter` → `@Composable fun Counter()`. `state` →
    `remember { mutableStateOf(...) }`. `Column(gap:)` →
    `Column(verticalArrangement = spacedBy(...))`.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

## Why two modes?

The dev loop needs liveness (patch, don't recompile); the shipped product
needs zero runtime overhead (native codegen). Keeping a single IR as the
contract means the dev experience and the release binary are provably the
same program — which is exactly what the parity harness proves: it captures
traces from both tiers and checks their equivalence in CI.

## Platform status within the tiers

The two hosts converge at different speeds, and the project is explicit
about it:

- **Android dev renders declaratively.** The dev tier drives the same
  declarative components the release codegen emits.
- **iOS dev is still imperative (UIKit).** Convergence to the declarative
  tier is gated on measurement (ADR-0048) — the migration happens when the
  numbers support it, not by decree.
- **Release is native on both platforms.** SwiftUI and Compose codegen
  output is the shipped artifact either way.

<Aside type="note">Node identity is what makes the two tiers equivalent in
practice: the codegen backends thread the same stable node IDs the dev VM
used, so generated views keep the exact identity the reconciler matched
during development. See [Architecture](/explanation/architecture/).</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Ship a native release](/guides/build-native/) — the operational how-to.
- [Project status](/explanation/project-status/) — what is verified today.


---

---
title: Project status
description: What is verified and runnable in Flux today — the dev hot-reload path, release codegen, tooling — and what is still converging.
type: explanation
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux is under active development, and the project is deliberate about
distinguishing what is proven from what is converging. This page tracks the
difference.

## Working today

- **Dev server (`flux dev`)** — binds a WebSocket patch channel on `:7331`
  and an HTTP asset server on `:7332` with a `/health` probe. Saves are
  diffed and shipped as binary patches; verified live against the repo's
  examples.
- **Host apps (iOS and Android)** — precompiled native hosts that connect
  to the dev server, run the embedded bytecode VM, and reconcile a shadow
  tree of native views. Default connection is `ws://127.0.0.1:7331`.
- **CLI** — `flux init` / `dev` / `build` / `fmt` / `lsp` / `doc` /
  `doctor`, all documented in the [CLI reference](/reference/cli/).
- **Release codegen** — `flux build ios|android` lowers `.flux` to
  idiomatic SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose, driven by the shared data-driven
  emitter with node-ID bridges on both backends.
- **Language server and editor tooling** — `flux-lsp` plus the VS Code
  extension with highlighting, diagnostics, hot-reload status, and run on
  device.
- **DevTools desktop app** — a gpui-based GUI rendering live telemetry over
  the same wire protocol.
- **Parity harness** — trace capture, reduction, and equivalence checking
  between dev-VM execution and release codegen output.
- **Perf harness and budgets** — the Save → pixels budget and per-stage
  latency budgets enforced by benchmarks.

## Converging

- **iOS declarative dev tier** — Android dev already renders through the
  same declarative components the release codegen emits; the iOS dev tier is
  imperative (UIKit) until convergence, and that migration is gated on
  measurement (ADR-0048).
- **Cross-host naming convergence** — adapter and capability naming is being
  aligned across hosts under a single convention (ADR-0049).

## How the project proves claims

Every claim above is backed by a mechanism, not a promise:

| Claim | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Dev and release are the same program | `flux-parity` equivalence checking in CI |
| Hosts behave identically | Byte-identical reconcile traces across Swift and Kotlin |
| The VM matches its contract | 92 golden ISA vectors shared by Rust, Swift, Kotlin |
| Hot reload stays fast | LANE-H harness with p50/p99 budgets on Save → pixels |
| Regressions fail loudly | 19 GitHub Actions workflows guard `main` |

## Architecture decisions

Every non-obvious choice is recorded as an ADR in the repository under
[`docs/adr/`](https://github.com/elcoosp/flux/tree/main/docs/adr) — 40 MADR
records through ADR-0059, from gas accounting to wire protocol v3. They stay
in the repository (not copied into this site) so the source of truth is one
file per decision, versioned next to the code that implements it.

<Aside type="caution">The project does not ship a runtime interpreter in
release builds. If a proposal adds one, it needs an ADR and a budget — the
release artifact is native code, full stop.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Dev vs release](/explanation/dev-vs-release/) — the reasoning behind the
  two tiers.
- [Testing and benchmarks](/guides/testing-and-benchmarks/) — run the
  mechanisms yourself.

---
title: Reactivity and host-authoritative state
description: The SolidJS-style signal graph, the host-authoritative state invariant (ADR-0027), and how a tap becomes exactly one update — independent of tree size.
type: explanation
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux's reactivity is **SolidJS-style**: a fine-grained dependency graph over
signals, not a virtual-diffing re-render loop. And Flux's state is
**host-authoritative**: the server never owns runtime signal values — it
ships structure (the IR) and deltas (patches), while the host owns the
signal graph, evaluates handlers, and reconciles the view.

## The invariant

> After a dispatch writes signal set `S`, the only nodes whose rendered
> output may change are (a) nodes whose prop/control expressions read some
> `s ∈ S`, and (b) nodes built/destroyed/reordered by keyed structural
> diffs triggered by (a). Everything else must be untouched.

This invariant is normative (ADR-0027), and it is what makes a 1,000-node
tree cost **one update** when you tap a counter bound to a single signal —
independent of tree size.

## How a dispatch flows

1. **Dispatch** — a tap evaluates the handler closure in the host VM,
   writing one or more signals (for example `count = count + 1`).
2. **Signals** — the VM reports the written signal ids, sorted ascending,
   as the `signals` trace event.
3. **Dirty set** — the host intersects the written signals with each node's
   `signal_deps`, emitting a `dirty` list in `(depth asc, id asc)` order.
4. **Update** — only the dirty nodes re-materialize their props and fire
   `update`. Clean siblings are untouched.
5. **Step end** — cumulative counters close the step: `built`, `updated`,
   `skipped_unchanged`, `detached`, `prop_materializations`.

A handler that writes a signal nothing reads produces `dirty: []` and zero
update/build/detach events — the `noop_dispatch` golden scenario pins this.

## Consequences

- **Patches are minimal.** A `count = count + 1` tap produces an `Update`
  patch addressed to the dirty node(s) only, never a re-send of the whole
  tree.
- **Trace parity is observable.** Because state is host-owned and
  deterministic, the same frame + dispatch script run against Swift and
  Kotlin yields byte-identical traces — that is the parity harness's job.
- **The server round-trip is on its way out.** Phase 3 of ADR-0027 ships
  prop thunks to the host, so the per-tap server round-trip and the
  `currentFrame()` reconstruction disappear entirely; the host recomputes
  from the dirty set.

## What this rules out

<Aside type="caution">The reconciler must not subscribe to the signal graph
as an observer — that double-fires. It consumes the VM outcome (ADR-0027
records this as explicitly out of scope).</Aside>

The same discipline explains the fault policy you meet in practice: when a
handler faults, the node keeps its prior props (render stale, never blank),
and the error surfaces through the overlay and the trace — the view is
never torn down.

## Where to see it

The counter example is the canonical demonstration: one signal, one
dependent `Text`, and a tap that costs exactly one update while the `Column`
and `Button` skip unchanged. The [todo tutorial](/tutorials/todo-app/) shows
the same mechanics with lists and routing layered on top.

## Next steps

- [Dev vs release](/explanation/dev-vs-release/) — how the two execution
  tiers share this machinery.
- [Architecture](/explanation/architecture/) — the crates that implement
  the graph and the dirty set.


---

---
title: The wire, explained
description: Why Flux talks binary over WebSocket, how BLAKE3 content addressing keeps patches tiny, and why the dirty set decides what ships.
type: explanation
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux talks to the host over a **binary wire protocol** (Appendix D), not
JSON. This page explains the reasoning; the byte-level layout lives in the
[wire protocol reference](/reference/wire-protocol/).

## Why binary

The patch channel carries frames on every save — potentially many per
minute during a hot-reload session, each on a device that is simultaneously
running your UI. A text format would spend its bytes on quotes, braces, and
field names. The binary protocol spends them on structure:

- All multi-byte integers are little-endian.
- A fixed 16-byte header opens every frame: magic `0x465C5558` (`"FLUX"`),
  version, sequence number, flags, and the entry counts.
- Variable data follows: patches, handler definitions, and interned strings.

## Why content addressing

Every prop, closure, and node is content-addressed by a **BLAKE3 hash**.
For each item in a frame, the server checks the host's cache: if the hash is
present, it sends only the 8-byte hash; if not, it sends the full data and
the host caches it.

The consequences are the patch economics you observe in practice:

- After the initial `Init` frame, more than 90% of props and closures are
  cache hits.
- A handler-body edit is typically a few hundred bytes on the wire.
- Interned strings ship once in a string-table delta and are referenced by
  id thereafter.

## Why the dirty set decides

The server does not guess what changed. It computes
`dirty = ⋃ dependents[S]` — the union of every node that depends on a
written signal (ADR-0027) — and emits **Update** patches addressed only to
dirty nodes, plus structural patches (`Insert` / `Remove` / `Reorder`) where
control props actually changed. Everything else stays out of the frame,
which is how a tap in a 1,000-node tree costs one update.

## Flags and liveness

The header's flag bits make the channel self-describing: `full_tree` marks
the initial snapshot, `heartbeat` keeps the connection observable, `error`
frames carry failure states, and the delta flags announce which tables
(state, source maps, strings) accompany the patches. A host that cannot
support the advertised protocol version rejects the handshake rather than
misinterpreting frames — protocol v3 (ADR-0059) widened the length prefixes
for user-authored collections to u32 for exactly this kind of
forward-compatibility discipline.

<Aside type="note">The DevTools desktop app (`flux-devtools-ui`, gpui-based)
subscribes to the same wire protocol and renders live telemetry from it —
one protocol, two consumers (ADR-0039, ADR-0041).</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Wire protocol reference](/reference/wire-protocol/) — the normative
  layouts, byte by byte.
- [VM instruction set](/reference/vm-isa/) — what the closures in a frame
  reference.

---
title: Ship a native release
description: Generate SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose sources with flux build ios|android, understand the output layout, and hand the sources to the native toolchains.
type: how-to
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

import { Aside, Code, TabItem, Tabs } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Development runs through the bytecode VM so saves hot-reload in milliseconds.
Release is different: `flux build` compiles the same IR to idiomatic native
source and ships no VM, no patch protocol, and no shadow tree. This guide
walks the release path per platform.

## Generate the native sources

Run the build from your project root and pick the platform:

<Tabs>
  <TabItem label="iOS">
    <Code lang="bash" code={`flux build ios`} />
    Emits `platforms/ios/Generated/main.swift`.
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Android">
    <Code lang="bash" code={`flux build android`} />
    Emits `platforms/android/Generated/main.kt`.
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

Both targets use `--root <path>` if you build a project elsewhere, matching
`flux dev`.

## What the output looks like

For the canonical counter (see the
[counter walkthrough](/tutorials/your-first-app/)) the emitted code is the
plain native equivalent of your `.flux`:

- `compo Counter` becomes `struct Counter: View` (SwiftUI) and
  `@Composable fun Counter()` (Compose).
- `state count` becomes `@State private var count: Int = 0` and
  `var count by remember { mutableStateOf<Int>(0) }`.
- `Column gap: 8.0` becomes `VStack(spacing:)` and
  `Column(verticalArrangement = spacedBy(8.dp))`.

There is no interpreter in the shipped app — the generated code is ordinary
SwiftUI and Compose that you review, version, and compile like any other
native source.

## Hand the sources to the toolchain

If `xcodebuild` or `gradle` is present on your machine, `flux build` suggests
the next build step after emitting the sources. Otherwise, compile them in
your app target like any other generated source:

- **iOS** — add the generated Swift files to your app target and build with
  Xcode as usual.
- **Android** — include the generated Kotlin files in your module's source
  set and build with Gradle.

## Why dev and release stay equivalent

Both execution tiers consume the same Reactive Tree IR. A parity harness
(`flux-parity`) captures traces from dev-VM execution and from release
codegen output and proves their equivalence in CI — the two paths are
verified, not assumed. See [Dev vs release](/explanation/dev-vs-release/) for
the reasoning and the current platform status.

<Aside type="note">On Android, the dev tier already renders through the same
declarative components the release codegen emits. The iOS dev tier is
imperative (UIKit) while convergence to the declarative tier is gated on
measurement (ADR-0048) — release output is SwiftUI on both tiers.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Formatting and CI gates](/guides/formatting-and-ci/) to keep generated
  input canonical.
- [Project status](/explanation/project-status/) for what is verified today.


---

---
title: Use platform capabilities
description: Call Camera, Storage, Router, Clipboard, and Location through the versioned capability contract — result cells, permission gating, and error handling.
type: how-to
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Platform services — storage, camera, clipboard, location — are not compiled
into your UI tree. They are **capabilities**: versioned contracts with stable,
deterministically derived identifiers, resolved identically on the dev server
and on both native hosts. This guide shows how to call them and how their
errors surface.

## The capability surface

The stable capability identifiers are declared in
[`stdlib/capabilities.flux`](https://github.com/elcoosp/flux/blob/main/stdlib/capabilities.flux)
and mirrored by the host capability registries:

| Capability | ID | Example method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Camera` | 1 | capture |
| `Storage` | 2 | `removeItem` (method 3) |
| `Router` | 3 | `navigate` (method 1 — drives the visible screen) |
| `Clipboard` | 4 | copy / paste |
| `Location` | 5 | current position |
| … | up through 11 | see `stdlib/capabilities.flux` |

Capability ids are derived deterministically and never hand-assigned — a
hand-assigned id desyncs the server and host registries and fails the parity
guards in CI.

## Call a capability from a handler

`CALL_CAP` is the mechanism; you reach it through the stdlib surface. The todo
app's Reset button clears the list and removes the persisted copy:

<Code lang="rust" code={`Button text: "Reset", onPress: || {
    tasks.clear()
    Storage.removeItem(key: "todos")
}`} />

`Storage.removeItem` is capability 2, method 3. The call carries its
arguments as a record and returns a **result cell**:

| Cell state | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Ready` | The call completed; the value is available. |
| `Pending` | An async capability is in flight; render your loading state. |
| `Error` | The call failed or was denied; the error carries the reason. |

A synchronous capability settles the cell before the call returns. An async
one leaves it `Pending`, and an injected `AsyncResolver` settles it when the
platform responds — the result is threaded back onto the reactive dispatcher,
so you never write signals from a background thread yourself.

## Render the pending and error states

Because the cell is a value in the signal graph, you render its states with
ordinary expressions:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo Profile
    state name: Option[String] = None
    Column gap: 8.0
        Text text: name ?? "Loading..."`} />

The `??` fallback covers `Pending` and empty results. For explicit error
handling, branch on the cell state and surface the reason in your UI —
capability errors are data, not exceptions.

## Handle permission denial

Capabilities gated behind OS permissions (Camera, Location, Notifications)
report a denial through the error path. The call **never crashes** the app:

- The host surfaces the system permission prompt when the capability needs
  one.
- A denied call renders as an on-device red banner and records an error in
  the trace; the denied call does not run.
- Re-invoke the handler after the user grants the permission.

The error payload names the numeric `cap_id` / `method_id`, the resolved
`cap_name` / `method_name` when registered, the required OS permission, and a
human-readable `why` — see the
[troubleshooting guide](/guides/troubleshooting/) for the full shapes.

<Aside type="note">The canonical machine-readable surface is emitted by the
CLI: `flux doc` prints the JSON schema of the stdlib API, capabilities
included. Keep it open while you wire calls.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Capability reference](/reference/capabilities/) for the id/method tables
  and the result-cell model.
- [State management](/guides/state-management/) for the async data patterns
  built on result cells.


---

---
title: Run and configure the dev server
description: Configure flux dev — ports, health probe, LAN exposure, and pairing tokens for the hot-reload loop.
type: how-to
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The dev server (`flux dev`) is your constant companion while you build a Flux
app: it watches, parses, type-checks, lowers, and diffs your `.flux` sources,
then ships binary patches to the connected host apps. This guide covers every
knob it exposes.

## Start the server on the defaults

Run it from your project root (or point it anywhere with `--root`):

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux dev
# Listening on ws://127.0.0.1:7331`} />

The defaults serve a project in the current directory, bound to localhost:

| Flag | Default | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--root <path>` | `.` | Project root to watch and serve |
| `--ws-host <addr>` | `127.0.0.1` | WebSocket bind address |
| `--ws-port <port>` | `7331` | Patch channel to the host apps |
| `--http-port <port>` | `7332` | HTTP asset server |
| `--token <secret>` | unset | Require a pairing token in the `Hello` handshake |

The same defaults live in `flux.toml` under `[dev]`, so a checked-in project
configures its ports for every contributor. See the
[flux.toml reference](/reference/flux-toml/).

## Verify the server is healthy

The asset server exposes a health probe:

<Code lang="bash" code={`curl http://127.0.0.1:7332/health`} />

<Code lang="text" code={`ok`} />

## Serve a physical device over the LAN

Simulators and emulators reach `127.0.0.1` on your machine; a physical device
cannot. Expose the server on your LAN and point the host app at your machine's
LAN IP:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux dev --ws-host 0.0.0.0`} />

In the host app, set the server address to `ws://192.168.1.42:7331`, replacing
the IP with the address of the machine running `flux dev`. The Android host
stores this in its resources; the iOS host takes it in its connection screen.

## Require a pairing token

An open dev loop on localhost is safe by default. A LAN-exposed server must
authenticate the hosts that push bytecode to it:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux dev --ws-host 0.0.0.0 --token <secret>`} />

The host presents its token during the `Hello` handshake (wire protocol
Appendix D, pairing/auth section). Hosts read their token from:

- the `FLUX_DEV_TOKEN` environment variable, or
- `[dev] token` in `flux.toml`.

A host without the token is rejected at the handshake and receives no frames.

<Aside type="caution">Never run `--ws-host 0.0.0.0` without `--token` on a
shared network. Any device on the LAN can then connect and receive your
source-derived frames.</Aside>

## What the server does on save

Every save triggers the full pipeline — you never restart anything:

1. Parse and type-check every `.flux` file. Diagnostics appear in the server
   log with source spans.
2. Lower the program to the Reactive Tree IR.
3. Diff the new tree against the previous one.
4. Serialize the minimal edit script as a binary patch and send it over
   `:7331`.

A handler-body edit is typically a few hundred bytes on the wire because
props and closures are content-addressed (BLAKE3) and cached on the host
after the first `Init` frame. See [The wire, explained](/explanation/the-wire/).

## Next steps

- [Ship a native release](/guides/build-native/) when dev looks right.
- [Wire protocol reference](/reference/wire-protocol/) for the frames the
  server sends.


---

---
title: Set up editor tooling
description: Install the VS Code extension and use flux lsp for parse and type diagnostics on .flux sources.
type: how-to
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux ships a language server (`flux-lsp`, built on `async-lsp`) and a VS Code
extension that wraps it. Together they give you syntax highlighting,
diagnostics, hot-reload status, and a one-click run on device.

## Install the VS Code extension

The extension lives in the repository at
[`editors/vscode/`](https://github.com/elcoosp/flux/tree/main/editors/vscode):

<Code lang="bash" code={`cd editors/vscode
pnpm install`} />

Open the folder in VS Code and launch it as an extension development host
(press `F5`), or package it with `vsce` and install the produced `.vsix`.
The extension bundles the Flux TextMate grammar — the same grammar this docs
site uses for `flux` code blocks — so highlighting matches the CLI's view of
the language.

While the extension is active you get:

- **Syntax highlighting** for `.flux` sources.
- **Diagnostics** pushed from parse and type checks.
- **Hot-reload status** for the connected dev server.
- **"Run on device"** to point the current project at a connected host.

## Get diagnostics from the CLI

The same diagnostics are available headlessly through `flux lsp`. It parses
and type-checks one file and prints the findings as JSON:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux lsp src/main.flux`} />

The output carries each diagnostic's message, span, and hint, so you can pipe
it into review tooling:

<Code lang="json" code={`{ "diagnostics": [ { "message": "expected \`Int\`, got \`String\`", "span": { "file": "src/main.flux", "start": 214, "end": 228 }, "hint": "\`count\` was inferred as Int at line 18" } ] }`} />

On large files where you only need syntax errors, skip the type checker:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux lsp src/main.flux --no-types`} />

## How diagnostics reach your editor

Every error Flux produces carries a source `Span` — file, line, and column —
which is what makes the editor integration useful: you get caret-positioned
diagnostics instead of a log dump. The [troubleshooting
guide](/guides/troubleshooting/) explains what each diagnostic class means
and how to fix it.

<Aside type="tip">Run `flux doctor` when an editor session behaves oddly. It
checks the toolchain, stdlib parse health, and wire protocol version in one
shot.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Formatting and CI gates](/guides/formatting-and-ci/) to keep sources
  canonical before they reach review.
- [CLI reference](/reference/cli/) for the full `flux lsp` surface.


---

---
title: Format sources and gate CI
description: Enforce canonical style with flux fmt --check, catch environment drift with flux doctor --strict, and keep the repo's fmt/clippy gates green.
type: how-to
sidebar:
  order: 7
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux enforces canonical style and environment health mechanically, so reviews
argue about code instead of formatting. This guide covers the three gates you
run before opening a PR.

## Format `.flux` sources

`flux fmt` formats `.flux` files to canonical style. With no paths it formats
`main.flux` in the project root:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux fmt                       # format main.flux in place
flux fmt src/views.flux        # format specific files`} />

Gate a pipeline with `--check`: the files are verified but not written, and
the process exits non-zero when any file would change:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux fmt --check`} />

## Check environment health

`flux doctor` runs the environment health check: toolchain state, stdlib
parse health, wire protocol version, and — best effort — connected devices
and simulators:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux doctor`} />

It also runs the local structural checks: approved-dependency drift (the
repository vets dependencies through ADRs, and `flux doctor` reports
unapproved drift) and violations of the repository's documented house rules.

Use `--strict` to make advisory findings blocking, so the command can gate a
pre-commit hook:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux doctor --strict   # exits non-zero on any finding`} />

## Keep the Rust gates green

If you touch the Flux implementation itself, the repository's CI expects a
clean tree by these commands — never plain `cargo test`:

<Code lang="bash" code={`cargo fmt -- --check
cargo clippy -- -D warnings
cargo nextest run
cargo test --doc      # doctests: nextest does not run these`} />

| Command | Gate |
| --- | --- |
| `cargo fmt -- --check` | Formatting clean |
| `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` | No lints |
| `cargo nextest run` | Full suite (unit, property, snapshot) |
| `cargo test --doc` | Doctests |

Library crates forbid `unsafe_code`, production code contains no `unwrap` /
`expect` / `panic!`, and every error carries a source `Span` — the clippy and
nextest gates are how these rules stay true.

<Aside type="tip">`flux fmt --check` and `flux doctor --strict` are cheap.
Wire both into a pre-commit hook and CI fails on formatting or drift before a
human ever sees it.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Testing and benchmarks](/guides/testing-and-benchmarks/) for the five test
  layers behind `cargo nextest run`.
- [Project status](/explanation/project-status/) for the CI workflow map.


---

---
title: Migrate from Flutter
description: An honest map from Flutter widgets to Flux primitives — layout, state, async — and the gaps Flux does not cover yet.
type: how-to
sidebar:
  order: 10
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

If you come from Flutter, Flux's declarative component model feels familiar:
a tree of components, recomputed from state. The differences are structural —
Flux splits layout into a small set of primitives, keeps state in signals,
and ships native code instead of a rendering engine. This guide maps the
concepts and names the gaps plainly.

## Widget → component map

| Flutter | Flux | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Column(children: [...])` | `Column` | `gap` replaces `SizedBox` spacers between children |
| `Row(children: [...])` | `Row` | Same, horizontal |
| `Text('...')` | `Text` | Interpolate signals with `{expr}` |
| `ElevatedButton` / `TextButton` | `Button` | `onPress` takes a `Handler` closure |
| `TextField` | `TextInput` | Controlled: `text: $binding`, `onChangeText` |
| `Image.asset(...)` | `Image` | `source` takes an asset path |
| `Navigator` / `MaterialPageRoute` | `Router` + `Screen` | `RouterNav.navigate` swaps screens |
| `Stack` | `Stack` | Same name, same idea |
| `GridView` | `Grid` | `columns` and `gap` props |
| `Scaffold` | Compose it | Assemble a `Column`/`Row` root yourself |
| `Container` / `Padding` | Component props + `gap` | No standalone padding widget |

## State

| Flutter | Flux |
| --- | --- |
| `StatefulWidget` + `setState` | `compo` with `state` signals; assign in a handler |
| `ValueNotifier` / `ChangeNotifier` | A signal; derived `let` replaces `Selector` |
| `InheritedWidget` / `Provider` | A store `compo` lifted above consumers; values as props |
| `FutureBuilder` | A capability call returning a result cell (`Ready`/`Pending`/`Error`) |
| `StreamBuilder` | Not yet; async data flows through capabilities |

The mental shift: no rebuild-in-progress dance. Assignment writes a signal,
the dirty set is computed from the dependency graph, and only affected leaves
recompose. See [state management](/guides/state-management/).

## Lists and keys

| Flutter | Flux |
| --- | --- |
| `ListView` over data | `ForEach(tasks, key: fn(t) { t.label }) { item => … }` |
| `Key` / `ValueKey` | The `key` function argument |
| Mutate list + `setState` | `tasks.append(...)` / `tasks.remove(task)` / `tasks.clear()` |

Keyed reconciliation matches children by node ID, so rows reorder and patch
in place — scroll positions and field contents survive edits.

## What Flux does not cover yet

- **The full widget catalog.** Only stdlib primitives exist; richer themed
  widgets (cards, chips) are a design-tokens/theming roadmap item.
- **Implicit animations.** Animation primitives are a roadmap item; today you
  drive values through signals. An `Animate` primitive exists for signal-
  driven curves and durations.
- **Web and desktop targets.** Flux renders natively on iOS and Android
  only. For embedded web content there is a `WebHost` primitive.
- **Styling depth.** No arbitrary `style` objects; layout flows through
  `gap`/`alignment` and per-component props.

For the common screens — forms, navigation, lists, capability-backed data —
Flux covers the ground. Where a gap bites, reach for the `WebHost` escape
hatch or wait for the roadmap item rather than fighting the layout system.

<Aside type="note">Coming from React Native instead? The mapping is in
[Migrate from React Native](/guides/migrate-from-rn/).</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Build the todo app](/tutorials/todo-app/) to exercise the mapped concepts
  in a real app.
- [The stdlib reference](/reference/stdlib/) for every primitive's props.


---

---
title: Migrate from React Native
description: An honest map from React Native concepts to Flux primitives — component model, state, effects — and the gaps Flux does not cover yet.
type: how-to
sidebar:
  order: 9
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux is a write-once UI language that compiles to native iOS and Android. If
you know React Native, most of the vocabulary transfers with a syntax change.
This guide maps RN concepts to Flux primitives and names the gaps plainly:
Flux targets the common 90% of app screens — forms, navigation, state,
capabilities — not 100% of RN's surface.

## Component model

| React Native | Flux | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `function Component() { return <View>… }` | `compo Name` with an indented body | Children indent beneath a view call that carries a named prop |
| `<View style={{flexDirection:'column'}}>` | [`Column`](/guides/state-management/) | Flux splits RN's `View` into `Column`/`Row` by design |
| `<View style={{flexDirection:'row'}}>` | `Row` | Same split, horizontal |
| `<Text>` | `Text` | Interpolate signals with `{expr}` |
| `<Button>` | `Button` | `onPress` takes a `Handler` closure |
| `<TextInput>` | `TextInput` | Controlled: `text: $binding`, `onChangeText` |
| `<Image>` | `Image` | `source` takes an asset path |
| `react-navigation` | `Router` + `Screen` | Navigate via `RouterNav.navigate` |

The stdlib's public component names mirror RN naming deliberately (see
ADR-0053 on public-surface naming), so muscle memory survives the port.

## State

| React Native | Flux |
| --- | --- |
| `useState` | `state name: Type = initial` at the top of a `compo` |
| `setState(v)` | Assign the signal: `name = v` inside a handler |
| Derived value in render | A read-only `let` computed from signals |
| Context / Redux | A store `compo` lifted above consumers; values as props |

The mental shift: there is no re-render cycle to opt into. Assignment
propagates through the signal graph, and only the nodes that read the written
signal recompose. See [state management](/guides/state-management/).

## Lists and keys

| React Native | Flux |
| --- | --- |
| `.map` over data into elements | `ForEach(tasks, key: fn(t) { t.label }) { item => … }` |
| `key` prop | The `key` function argument |
| Mutate array + `setState` | `tasks.append(...)` / `tasks.remove(task)` / `tasks.clear()` |

The reconciler matches children by node ID and the key function, so existing
rows reorder and patch in place instead of rebuilding.

## Effects and async

| React Native | Flux |
| --- | --- |
| `useEffect(fetch)` | A capability call returning a result cell (`Ready`/`Pending`/`Error`) |
| Loading branches | Render from the cell: `name ?? "Loading..."` |
| Native modules | Capabilities with stable ids (Storage, Camera, Clipboard, Location…) |

There is no `async` keyword in handlers — async work settles through the
capability result cell, and results land back on the reactive dispatcher for
you. See [capabilities](/guides/capabilities/).

## What Flux does not cover yet

These gaps are real as of this writing — plan around them rather than
discovering them in review:

- **Stylesheets and flex props.** There is no `StyleSheet.create` or
  arbitrary `style` object. Layout is expressed through `Column`/`Row`
  `gap`/`alignment` and per-component props. Design tokens and theming are a
  roadmap item.
- **Third-party component libraries.** Only the stdlib primitives exist. For
  web content there is a `WebHost` primitive that embeds web views; deeper
  native interop is an escape-hatch concern.
- **Web target.** Flux renders natively on iOS and Android only. There is no
  web backend.

If your app depends heavily on one of these, hold off on the port — but the
common screens (forms, navigation, state, capability-backed data) transfer
directly.

<Aside type="note">The migration stories for Flutter live in a companion
guide: [Migrate from Flutter](/guides/migrate-from-flutter/).</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Build the todo app](/tutorials/todo-app/) to exercise the mapped concepts
  in a real app.
- [Troubleshooting](/guides/troubleshooting/) for the error shapes you meet
  during a port.


---

---
title: Navigate between screens
description: Build multi-screen apps with Router, Screen, and RouterNav — the route prop contract, initial routes, and capability-driven navigation.
type: how-to
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux ships navigation as part of the language: a `Router` declares the stack,
`Screen` children declare the routes, and `RouterNav.navigate` switches the
visible screen. This guide shows the working pattern from
`examples/router` and `examples/todo`.

## Declare a router with two screens

Every screen must carry a `route` prop, and the router names its first
screen:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo App
    Column gap: 8.0
        Router initialRouteName: "home"
            Screen route: "home"
                Column gap: 16.0
                    Text text: "Home"
                    Button text: "Go to Settings", onPress: || {
                        RouterNav.navigate("settings")
                    }
            Screen route: "settings"
                Column gap: 16.0
                    Text text: "Settings"
                    Button text: "Go to Home", onPress: || {
                        RouterNav.navigate("home")
                    }`} />

- `initialRouteName` names the screen shown at startup.
- `RouterNav.navigate("settings")` makes the screen whose `route` equals
  `"settings"` visible.
- Each screen owns its layout through its own layout component (`Column`).

<Aside type="caution">The prop name must be exactly `route`. The host reads
it by its hashed prop name (FNV-1a of `"route"`), so renaming it silently
breaks navigation — the contract is normative in the adapter appendices.</Aside>

## Keep screen state across navigation

The reconciler matches children by node ID, so an existing screen is
reordered, never recreated, across push/pop. State you keep in screen-level
signals survives navigation: a half-typed form stays filled when the user
switches screens and returns.

Model per-screen state with `state` declarations inside the screen's
components, and cross-screen state with a store lifted above the `Router`
(see [state management](/guides/state-management/)).

## Drive navigation from data

Navigation runs through the Router capability (capability 3, method 1), which
writes its argument to a well-known signal the host reconcilers observe. You
call it through `RouterNav.navigate` from any handler — buttons, pickers,
gesture callbacks — and the visible screen follows the value.

The todo app's About button is the minimal example:

<Code lang="rust" code={`Button text: "About", onPress: || { RouterNav.navigate("about") }`} />

## Structure of a multi-screen app

The `examples/todo` app shows the full shape: one screen renders the task
list and its input row, the second renders a static About screen, and both
live inside one `Router` at the root of the layout tree. Keep routers at the
root of a screen region and let components below stay route-unaware — they
receive data and emit handlers, exactly like any other component.

## Next steps

- [The todo tutorial](/tutorials/todo-app/) builds a two-screen app end to
  end.
- [The wire, explained](/explanation/the-wire/) explains why patches — not
  full tree re-sends — move screens.


---

---
title: Manage state
description: Patterns over the Flux signal graph — local signals, derived values, shared stores, controlled inputs, and async data through capabilities.
type: how-to
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux renders from a reactive signal graph. Every `state` declaration is a
signal, and an assignment inside a handler is the whole update: the UI
recomputes only the nodes that read the written signal. This guide gives
copy-paste patterns for the shapes you meet beyond the counter.

## Declare local state

Declare a signal at the top of a `compo`:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo Counter
    state count: Int = 0
    Column gap: 8.0
        Text text: "tapped {count} times"
        Button text: "Increment", onPress: || { count = count + 1 }`} />

The `$count: Int = 0` shorthand is equivalent — you meet it in the scaffold
and in `examples/counter`. Both forms create the same signal; pick one style
per codebase and keep it.

There is no separate `setState`. The assignment *is* the update, and the
assignment inside a handler propagates through the dependency graph before
the host reconciles the dirty set.

## Derive values instead of storing them

A value computed from other signals should be derived, not stored — two
signals that can disagree are a bug you have not met yet. Declare it as a
read-only `let` computed from signals:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo Cart
    state items: Int = 3
    state price: Float = 9.99
    let total: Float = items * price   // recomputed when items or price change
    Column
        Text text: "Total: {total}"`} />

Derivation recomputes when a written signal reaches it, and only the leaves
that read `total` recompose.

## Bind a text input both ways

`TextInput` is controlled: bind the signal with `$` and write the typed value
back in `onChangeText`:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo Composer
    state draft: String = ""
    Column gap: 8.0
        TextInput text: $draft, onChangeText: fn(v) { draft = v }, placeholder: "Say something"
        Button text: "Clear", onPress: || { draft = "" }`} />

The `$draft` binding keeps the field and the signal in lockstep, so the Clear
button empties the field by assigning the signal.

## Share state across components

Flux has no provider/context widget. For state shared across components, lift
a store component above its consumers and thread values down as props:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo SessionStore
    state token: Option[String] = None
    // actions are handlers that write the store's signals

compo App
    SessionStore
        // children read token/user via props threaded from here`} />

Keep stores small and explicit — one store per domain (auth, cart, settings),
mounted at the root `Router` or `Screen` that needs it. The signal graph is
shared across the whole app, so a store mounted high is visible to everything
mounted beneath it.

## Load async data through a capability

Handlers stay synchronous; async work goes through a capability call that
returns a result cell (`Ready` / `Pending` / `Error`). An async capability
leaves the cell `Pending`, and an injected resolver settles it when the
platform responds:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo Profile
    state name: Option[String] = None
    Column gap: 8.0
        Text text: name ?? "Loading..."
        Button text: "Load", onPress: || {
            // call the capability; the result cell settles and updates \`name\`
        }`} />

The `??` operator renders the fallback while the cell is pending. See
[Capabilities](/guides/capabilities/) for the call surface and permission
handling.

<Aside type="caution">Never write signals or mutate the shadow tree from
outside the reactive dispatcher. Capability results are threaded back onto
the dispatcher for you — keep it that way.</Aside>

## Pattern summary

- **Local**: `state` (or `$`) plus assignment in a handler.
- **Computed**: a `let` derived from signals, never a second signal.
- **Shared**: a store `compo` lifted above its consumers; values as props.
- **Input**: `$binding` on `TextInput` plus `onChangeText`.
- **Async**: capability call → result cell → signal update on resolve.

## Next steps

- [Navigation](/guides/navigation/) for multi-screen apps that share state.
- [Host-authoritative state](/explanation/reactivity/) for the invariant that
  makes one tap cost one update, independent of tree size.


---

---
title: Run tests and benchmarks
description: Exercise the five test layers — nextest, proptest, insta snapshots, criterion budgets, and the dev-vs-release parity harness.
type: how-to
sidebar:
  order: 8
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux's quality bar is mechanical: every public function has a test, and the
suite spans five layers. This guide shows how to run each layer and what it
proves.

## Run the full suite

The project's test runner is `cargo-nextest` — never plain `cargo test`:

<Code lang="bash" code={`cargo nextest run`} />

| Layer | Tool | What it proves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | `cargo nextest run` | Every function, edge cases, error paths |
| Property | `proptest` | Node-ID stability, diff minimality, round-trips |
| Snapshot | `insta` | Swift & Kotlin codegen output |
| Benchmark | `criterion` | Per-stage latency budgets |
| Parity | `tests/` | Dev VM execution equals release codegen |

Doctests run separately, because nextest does not execute them:

<Code lang="bash" code={`cargo test --doc`} />

## Check dev-vs-release parity

The parity harness (`flux-parity`) is the tool that keeps the two execution
tiers honest: it captures traces from dev-VM execution and from release
codegen, reduces them, and checks equivalence. Golden scenarios — including
a 1,000-node counter tree and no-op dispatches — live under `tests/` and run
in the `parity-check` CI workflow.

When you change lowering, differ, or codegen behavior, run the parity
scenarios before trusting your own tests:

<Code lang="bash" code={`cargo nextest run -p flux-parity`} />

## Validate against the golden ISA vectors

The shipping Swift (`FluxBytecodeVM`) and Kotlin VMs are validated against
**92 golden ISA vectors** under `tests/isa-vectors/`. The Rust VM oracle
(`flux-vm-ref`) is the behavioral reference for the instruction set, and the
vectors are shared by all three implementations, so a fault code change fails
everywhere at once.

## Measure against the latency budgets

The headline metric is the **Save → pixels** budget — the wall-clock a
developer feels during hot reload — measured end to end by the LANE-H
harness: a real `DevServer` plus a headless loopback WebSocket client, with
at least 50 edits per tree size, reported as p50/p99.

| Stage | Budget |
| --- | --- |
| Parse a 500-line file | < 5 ms |
| Diff a 50-node tree | < 1 ms |
| Serialize a 50-node patch | < 1 ms |
| VM eval per frame | < 2 ms |

Criterion benchmarks carry these budgets; the `benchmarks.yml` and
`perf-harness.yml` CI workflows run them:

<Code lang="bash" code={`cargo bench`} />

<Aside type="caution">Property-based and adversarial suites
(`proptest`, the wire fuzzer, the corruption tests) intentionally throw
garbage at the pipeline. A failure there means a real robustness bug, not a
bad seed — record the failing case, do not delete it from the corpus.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [The VM instruction set](/reference/vm-isa/) — the contract the golden
  vectors encode.
- [Formatting and CI gates](/guides/formatting-and-ci/) for the pre-commit
  gates that run before the suite.


---

---
title: Troubleshoot Flux errors
description: Diagnose Flux errors by class — compile (parse, type, lower), runtime VM faults, and capability denials — with the message shape, root cause, and fix for each.
type: how-to
sidebar:
  order: 11
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Every error Flux surfaces — in the dev server log, the on-device red banner,
or the CLI output — belongs to the unified error taxonomy: three classes,
each carrying a `what` / `where` / `why` / `how` payload. This guide is keyed
to that taxonomy so you can go from message to fix.

| Class | When it fires | Where you see it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Compile** | Parse, type-check, or lowering failure | Dev server log, `flux lsp`, VS Code |
| **Runtime** | VM fault during handler evaluation | On-device overlay, server log, trace |
| **Capability** | A `CALL_CAP` denied by the host or OS | On-device red banner, trace |

## Compile errors

Typical shape:

<Code lang="text" code={`[compile:Parse] expected \`Int\`, got \`String\` (hint: \`count\` was inferred as Int at line 18)
[compile:Type] …
[compile:Lower] …`} />

Each compile error carries a phase, a message, a `span` (file:line:col), and
an optional hint.

| Phase | What it means | Common cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Parse` | The parser rejected the source | Mixed indentation and braces, or a missing indent under a view call | Follow the indentation grammar; run `flux dev` and read the caret |
| `Type` | The type checker rejected an expression | A signal used as the wrong type, or a handler body that mismatches its prop type | Read the `hint` — it names the previously inferred type and location |
| `Lower` | The typed AST could not lower to the IR | A construct outside the supported surface | Simplify the expression; check `flux doc` for the supported surface |

**Fix path:** open the file:line:col from the `span`, read the `hint`, and
re-express the construct. Compile errors are deterministic — re-running
`flux dev` reproduces them exactly.

## Runtime (VM) errors

Typical shape:

<Code lang="text" code={`[runtime] gas budget exhausted at offset 42
[runtime] division by zero at offset 17`} />

Runtime errors wrap a stable VM fault kind, so the fault code is load-bearing
and asserted by the golden ISA vectors. The `offset` points at the offending
instruction, which tells you which Flux expression lowered to it.

### Gas budget exhausted

A handler ran for more than 100,000 instructions. Break the work into
smaller handlers, or remove an accidental infinite loop or unbounded
recursion.

### Memory pool exhausted

The 16 MiB frame memory pool ran out — usually large literals or deep frames.
Reduce the data held in handler scope; page large data through a capability
instead of inlining it.

### Index out of bounds

A list, record, or string index fell outside its bounds. Guard the index
before access — this is a logic bug in the handler.

### Null dereference

A field access was performed on `Null`. Check the value before field access,
or ensure the upstream signal is initialized; the `??` operator covers the
common fallback case.

### Invalid opcode dispatch

The dispatch byte was not a valid opcode — usually a corrupt or stale patch
frame. Restart `flux dev`. If it recurs, treat it as a wire or lowering bug
and file an issue with the frame bytes.

### Type mismatch

Operands did not match what the monomorphized opcode expects — `ADD_I64`
needs two integers, `ADD_F64` two floats. Align the operand types.

### Division by zero

Integer division or remainder by zero fails as an error, never a panic.
Guard the divisor before the `/` or `%` operation.

**Fix path:** the fault is deterministic and reproducible. The handler
bytecode around the reported offset maps back to a specific Flux expression —
fix that expression.

## Capability errors

Typical shape:

<Code lang="text" code={`[capability] \`Storage.removeItem\` (2/3): the OS grant \`.storage\` was not authorized for this capability call`} />

Capability errors carry the numeric `cap_id` / `method_id`, the resolved
`cap_name` / `method_name` when registered, the required OS permission, and a
human-readable `why`. They **never crash** the app — the denied call does not
run, and the host renders a red banner.

- **Root cause:** a capability call reached a service gated behind an OS
  permission the user has not granted (Camera, Location, Notifications).
- **Fix:** request and await the permission before calling the capability.
  The host surfaces the system prompt; re-invoke the handler after the grant
  resolves.

Capability ids are derived deterministically — see the
[capabilities reference](/reference/capabilities/) for the id table.

<Aside type="tip">Compile errors name a span, runtime errors name a bytecode
offset, capability errors name a cap/method pair. Read that locator first —
it is the fastest route from message to cause.</Aside>

## Still stuck?

- [Dev vs release](/explanation/dev-vs-release/) clarifies which execution
  tier produced the error.
- [The wire, explained](/explanation/the-wire/) helps when frames look
  corrupt.
- [State management](/guides/state-management/) covers state that refuses to
  update.

---
title: Flux
description: Flux is a write-once UI language for native iOS and Android — hot-reload .flux on device, then ship SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose from the same source.
template: splash
type: explanation
sidebar:
  order: 0
hero:
  image:
    file: ../../assets/logo.png
    alt: Logo
  title: "Flux"
  tagline: Write once. Render native on iOS and Android.
  actions:
    - text: Start the tutorial
      link: /tutorials/your-first-app/
      icon: right-arrow
    - text: Browse the CLI reference
      link: /reference/cli/
      icon: document
      variant: minimal
---

import { Card, CardGrid, LinkButton, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Flux is a write-once UI language for native iOS and Android. You author your UI
in `.flux` files. In development, a precompiled host app receives binary patches
over WebSocket and hot-reloads your UI in milliseconds. In release, the exact
same source compiles to idiomatic **SwiftUI** and **Jetpack Compose**. No
webview. No JavaScript bridge. No interpreter in production.

| | Traditional cross-platform | Flux |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Render target | WebView / canvas | Real `UIView` / Compose `View` |
| Hot reload | Full rebuild or JS eval | Binary IR patch over WebSocket |
| Release build | Interpreter shipped in prod | SwiftUI / Compose codegen |
| State | Framework-locked | SolidJS-style signal graph over one shared IR |

The development loop and the release artifact come from the **same Reactive
Tree IR**. You iterate against a fast bytecode VM host during development and
ship platform-native code in release — no fork in the road, no "dev looks
different from prod". A parity harness (`flux-parity`) continuously proves that
dev-VM execution and release codegen stay equivalent, so the two paths are
verified, not assumed.

<CardGrid stagger>
  <Card title="One language, two native apps" icon="document">
    Author your UI once in `.flux`. A precompiled host app renders it on iOS
    and Android in dev; release builds compile the same IR to SwiftUI and
    Jetpack Compose.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Live hot reload" icon="rocket">
    Save a `.flux` file and the dev server parses, type-checks, lowers, diffs,
    and ships a binary patch in milliseconds. The on-device tree updates in
    place.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Real tooling" icon="puzzle">
    A CLI, a hot-reload dev server with pairing tokens, a language server with
    a VS Code extension, a formatter, and a gpui DevTools desktop app.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Spec-driven" icon="open-book">
    Every non-obvious choice is justified in an Architecture Decision Record —
    40 ADRs, normative wire and ISA appendices, and enforced parity tests.
  </Card>
</CardGrid>

<LinkButton href="/tutorials/todo-app/" icon="right-arrow">Start the tutorial</LinkButton>

## Choose your path

<LinkCard title="Build your first Flux app" href="/tutorials/your-first-app/" description="A guided tutorial: build the CLI, scaffold a project, hot-reload on a device, and ship a native release." />
<LinkCard title="Run and configure the dev server" href="/guides/dev-server/" description="Ports, LAN exposure, and pairing tokens for the hot-reload loop." />
<LinkCard title="Language and stdlib reference" href="/reference/language/" description="The complete .flux surface: components, signals, closures, and types." />
<LinkCard title="How Flux works" href="/explanation/architecture/" description="The parse → typecheck → lower → diff → patch → VM pipeline, explained." />

## What you need

The Rust toolchain builds everything on the CLI side. Xcode (iOS 16+
deployment target) and the Android SDK are required only for the host apps.
Walk through the [first-app tutorial](/tutorials/your-first-app/) for the full
setup.
