---
title: Capabilities reference
description: The versioned capability contract — stable ids, methods, result cells, permission gating, and how async results return to the signal graph.
type: reference
sidebar:
  order: 7
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Platform services are exposed to `.flux` programs through a **versioned
capability contract**: a registry of capabilities and methods with stable,
deterministically derived numeric ids, resolved identically on the dev
server and on both native hosts. The declarations live in
[`stdlib/capabilities.flux`](https://github.com/elcoosp/flux/blob/main/stdlib/capabilities.flux)
and the host registries mirror them; the IDL is kept in sync by generated
code (ADR-0045, ADR-0058).

## Capability ids

| Capability | ID | Known method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Camera` | 1 | capture |
| `Storage` | 2 | `removeItem` (method 3) |
| `Router` | 3 | `navigate` (method 1) |
| `Clipboard` | 4 | copy / paste |
| `Location` | 5 | current position |
| … | up through 11 | see `stdlib/capabilities.flux` |

Capability ids are derived deterministically and never hand-assigned — a
hand-assigned id desyncs the server and host registries, and the parity
guards fail the build when the tables drift.

A capability call in the wire/VM is `CALL_CAP`; it carries the capability
and method ids plus the argument record.

## Result cells

`CALL_CAP` returns a **result-cell signal**. The cell is part of the
reactive graph, so you render its states with ordinary expressions:

| State | Meaning | Typical render |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Ready` | The call completed | The value |
| `Pending` | An async call is in flight | `value ?? "Loading..."` |
| `Error` | The call failed or was denied | Your error UI |

A synchronous capability settles the cell before the call returns. An async
capability leaves it `Pending` and an injected `AsyncResolver` settles it
when the platform responds (ADR-0044, ADR-0045).

## Async delivery

Async results are threaded back onto the reactive dispatcher by the host —
you never write signals from a background thread. When a cell settles, the
host recomputes the dirty set from the written signal exactly as for any
other dispatch, and only the nodes that read the cell recompose.

## Permission gating

Capabilities backed by OS permissions (Camera, Location, Notifications) are
gated by the host:

- The host surfaces the system permission prompt when required.
- A denied call produces a **capability error** — it never crashes the app.
  The denied call does not run, and the host renders the on-device red
  banner.
- The error payload names `cap_id` / `method_id`, the resolved
  `cap_name` / `method_name`, the required OS permission, and a
  human-readable `why`.

See the [troubleshooting guide](/guides/troubleshooting/) for the fix path,
and the [capabilities how-to](/guides/capabilities/) for call patterns.

<Aside type="note">`flux doc` prints the machine-readable schema of the
capability surface along with the rest of the stdlib — keep it open while
wiring calls.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Capabilities how-to](/guides/capabilities/) for copy-paste call patterns.
- [Wire protocol reference](/reference/wire-protocol/) for how capability
  results travel.


---

---
title: CLI reference
description: The flux command-line interface — init, dev, build, lsp, fmt, doc, doctor — with every flag, default, and environment variable.
type: reference
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The `flux` binary is the developer CLI for the Flux UI language: it scaffolds
projects, runs the hot-reload dev server, codegens native apps, and inspects
the stdlib and environment. The surface below is generated from the CLI's
command definitions in `crates/flux-cli`.

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux <command> [flags]`} />

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `flux init <name>` | Scaffold a new Flux project at `<name>/` |
| `flux dev` | Start the hot-reload dev server |
| `flux build <platform>` | Codegen the project for a native platform |
| `flux lsp <file>` | Emit parse + type-check diagnostics as JSON |
| `flux fmt [files…]` | Format `.flux` sources to canonical style |
| `flux doc` | Emit a JSON schema of the stdlib API |
| `flux doctor` | Run the environment health check |

## `flux init <name>`

Scaffolds `<name>/` with `main.flux` (a stateful counter component),
`flux.toml`, and `.fluxignore`.

| Argument | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Project name; also the directory that is created |

## `flux dev`

| Flag | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--root <path>` | `.` | Project root to watch and serve |
| `--ws-host <addr>` | `127.0.0.1` | WebSocket bind host; `0.0.0.0` exposes the LAN |
| `--ws-port <port>` | `7331` | WebSocket patch channel |
| `--http-port <port>` | `7332` | HTTP asset server |
| `--token <secret>` | unset | Require the token in the host `Hello` handshake |

Hosts authenticate with the token read from `FLUX_DEV_TOKEN` or
`[dev] token` in `flux.toml`. Without `--token`, localhost keeps an open dev
loop. See the [dev server guide](/guides/dev-server/) for the operational
details.

## `flux build <platform>`

| Argument / flag | Values | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `platform` | `ios`, `android` | Target platform (positional) |
| `--root <path>` | `.` | Project root to build |

Emits generated sources to `platforms/<platform>/Generated/` (`main.swift`
/ `main.kt`), then invokes the native toolchain when present.

## `flux lsp <file>`

| Argument / flag | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `file` | required | The `.flux` source file to analyze |
| `--no-types` | off | Parse diagnostics only — the fast path for large files |

Prints parse and type-check diagnostics as JSON; every diagnostic carries a
span and an optional hint.

## `flux fmt [files…]`

| Argument / flag | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `files…` | `main.flux` | Files to format; with no paths, formats `main.flux` in the project root |
| `--check` | off | Verify without writing; exits non-zero when a file would change (CI gating) |

## `flux doc`

No flags. Prints the JSON schema of the stdlib API to stdout — the
source-of-truth surface behind the [stdlib reference](/reference/stdlib/).

## `flux doctor`

| Flag | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--strict` | off | Exit non-zero on advisory findings so the command can gate a pre-commit hook |

Checks toolchain state, stdlib parse health, wire protocol version, and
(best-effort) connected devices and simulators, plus the local structural
checks: approved-dependency drift and house-rule violations.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Used by | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLUX_DEV_TOKEN` | Host apps | Pairing token for the dev server `Hello` handshake |
| `RUST_LOG` | CLI | Tracing filter; defaults to `info` |
| `NO_COLOR` | CLI | Disables ANSI colors in output |

<Aside type="note">ANSI colors are emitted only when stdout is a real terminal
and `NO_COLOR` is unset, so piped and redirected output stays plain text.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [flux.toml reference](/reference/flux-toml/) for the project manifest.
- [Dev server guide](/guides/dev-server/) for day-to-day operation.


---

---
title: flux.toml reference
description: The Flux project manifest — project name and entry, dev server ports, and pairing token configuration.
type: reference
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

`flux.toml` is the project manifest at the root of every Flux project. It
configures the CLI and the dev server, and it is versioned with your project
so every contributor gets the same ports and settings.

## Format

<Code lang="toml" code={`[project]
name = "todo"
entry = "main.flux"

[dev]
ws_port = 7331
http_port = 7332`} />

## Keys

### `[project]`

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | — | Project name |
| `entry` | string | — | The entry `.flux` file, usually `main.flux` |

### `[dev]`

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ws_port` | integer | `7331` | WebSocket patch channel port |
| `http_port` | integer | `7332` | HTTP asset server port (serves `/health`) |
| `token` | string | unset | Pairing token hosts must present in the `Hello` handshake |

`flux dev` reads these values, and its `--ws-port` / `--http-port` /
`--token` flags override them for a single run.

## Pairing tokens

Hosts read their token from the `FLUX_DEV_TOKEN` environment variable or
from `[dev] token` in this file, and present it during the `Hello` handshake
when the server was started with `--token`. Set the same secret in both
places when you expose the dev server on a LAN — see the
[dev server guide](/guides/dev-server/).

<Aside type="caution">A token in `flux.toml` is versioned with the project.
For anything beyond a local, throwaway pairing secret, prefer
`FLUX_DEV_TOKEN` in your shell or device configuration.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [CLI reference](/reference/cli/) for the flags that override these keys.
- [Wire protocol reference](/reference/wire-protocol/) for the handshake the
  token guards.


---

---
title: Language reference
description: The .flux surface — components, records, signals, closures, view calls, interpolation, operators, and types.
type: reference
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This page is the reference for the `.flux` language surface. Grammar
extensions and their rationale are recorded as ADRs (the parser grammar is
normative in the specification's appendices); this page presents the surface
you write every day.

## Program structure

A `.flux` file contains top-level declarations:

| Declaration | Syntax | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Component | `compo Name(props…)` | A UI component with an indented body |
| Record | `record Name { field: Type, … }` | A data type with named fields |
| Const binding | `Name.field = expr` | A top-level constant (used by `color.flux`, `font.flux`) |

## Components (`compo`)

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo TaskRow(task: Task, tasks: List[Task])
    Row gap: 8.0
        Text text: task.label
        Button text: "Remove", onPress: || { tasks.remove(task) }`} />

- A `compo` declares typed props in parentheses and owns an indented body.
- Children indent beneath a view call that carries at least one named prop —
  this is what lets the indentation-delimited grammar distinguish a child
  block from a sibling.
- Prop defaults are written inline: `enabled: Bool = true`.

## State signals

Two equivalent forms declare a reactive signal at the top of a `compo`:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo Counter
    $count: Int = 0            // sigil form

compo Counter2
    state count: Int = 0       // keyword form`} />

An assignment inside a handler writes the signal. Written signals propagate
through the dependency graph, and only nodes whose props read a written
signal re-materialize — see [host-authoritative state](/explanation/reactivity/).

## Derived values (`let`)

<Code lang="rust" code={`let total: Float = items * price`} />

A `let` declares a read-only binding computed from signals. It recomputes
when a written signal reaches it; do not mirror it into a second signal.

## Closures

| Form | Shape | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zero-argument | `\|\| { count = count + 1 }` | Handler props (`onPress`, `onChange`) |
| Named parameter | `fn(v) { newTask = v }` | Callbacks that receive the event value |
| Key function | `fn(t) { t.label }` | `ForEach` keys |
| Lambda child | `{ item => TaskRow(task: item, …) }` | `ForEach` item rendering |

## View calls and props

A view call names a stdlib component and carries named props:

<Code lang="rust" code={`TextInput text: $newTask, onChangeText: fn(v) { newTask = v }, placeholder: "What needs doing?"`} />

- Props are comma-separated `name: value` pairs on one line.
- `text: $signal` two-way binds the prop to a signal (used by `TextInput`).
- Handlers are closures; their bodies compile to bytecode the host VM runs.

## Interpolation and operators

<Code lang="rust" code={`Text text: "tapped {count} times"`} />

`{expr}` inside a string literal interpolates a value into the prop. The
expression surface includes arithmetic, comparison, optional chaining with
`?.`, and the `??` fallback operator:

<Code lang="rust" code={`Text text: name ?? "Loading..."`} />

## Control flow: ForEach and routing

<Code lang="rust" code={`ForEach(tasks, key: fn(t) { t.label }) { item => TaskRow(task: item, tasks: tasks) }
Router initialRouteName: "tasks"
    Screen route: "tasks"
        …`} />

`ForEach` renders a list with a key function; `Router`/`Screen`/`RouterNav`
drive navigation. See the [navigation guide](/guides/navigation/).

## Types

| Type | Written as | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primitives | `String`, `Int`, `Float`, `Bool` | |
| List | `List[Task]` | Mutable through `append`/`remove`/`clear` |
| Optional | `Option[String]` | Unwrap with `??` fallback |
| Record | declared `record` types | Field access with `.` |
| Color | `Color` | Presets `red`/`green`/`blue`/`black`/`white` |
| Font | `Font`, `Weight`, `Style` | Presets `body`/`title`/`caption` |

The stdlib value types live in `stdlib/prelude.flux` (`Option`,
`Alignment`, `Overflow`, `KeyboardType`, `ContentMode`, `Ref`, `Handler`)
and `stdlib/traits.flux` (`Numeric`, `Eq`, `Show`).

<Aside type="note">Grammar gaps the stdlib needed — top-level `Name.field =
expr` constants, prop defaults, record literals in value position, and
symbolic operator method names — are all closed and recorded in
ADR-0037/ADR-0035; no gap remains open.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [The stdlib reference](/reference/stdlib/) for every component's props.
- [The CLI reference](/reference/cli/) to run the language.


---

---
title: Standard library reference
description: Every Flux stdlib component with its real prop contract — layout, text, controls, input, navigation, overlays, motion — plus value types and presets.
type: reference
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

import { Aside, Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The Flux standard library declares every UI primitive as a `.flux` file under
[`stdlib/`](https://github.com/elcoosp/flux/tree/main/stdlib). The
declarations are contracts: component bodies are supplied natively by the
platform adapters in dev and by the SwiftUI/Compose backends in release, but
the props and types you see below are the single shared surface.

The canonical machine-readable form of this page is the CLI:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux doc`} />

`flux doc` prints the JSON schema of the stdlib API to stdout.

## Layout

| Component | Props | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Column` | `gap: Float = 0.0`, `alignment: Option[Alignment] = None` | Vertical stack |
| `Row` | `gap: Float = 0.0`, `alignment: Option[Alignment] = None` | Horizontal stack |
| `Stack` | `gap: Float = 0.0`, `alignment: Option[Alignment] = None` | Z-stacked children |
| `Grid` | `columns: Int = 2`, `gap: Float = 0.0` | Grid layout |
| `ScrollView` | `orientation: Option[String] = None` | Scrollable container |
| `Spacer` | `flex: Float = 1.0` | Flexible space |
| `SafeArea` | `edges: Option[String] = None` | Inset children by safe areas |

## Text and media

| Component | Props | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Text` | `text: String`, `font: Option[Font] = None`, `size: Option[Float] = None`, `color: Option[Color] = None`, `alignment: Option[Alignment] = None`, `maxLines: Option[Int] = None` | String interpolation via `{expr}` |
| `Image` | `source: String`, `width: Option[Float] = None`, `height: Option[Float] = None`, `resizeMode: Option[String] = Some("fill")` | Renders a bitmap asset |
| `WebHost` | `src: String` | Embedded web view — the native-interop escape hatch |

## Controls

| Component | Props | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Button` | `text: String`, `onPress: Handler`, `enabled: Bool = true`, `color: Option[Color] = None` | Tappable action |
| `Toggle` | `value: Bool = false`, `onValueChange: Handler = fn() {}`, `enabled: Bool = true` | Boolean control |
| `Switch` | `value: Bool = false`, `onChange: Handler = fn() {}`, `enabled: Bool = true` | Boolean switch |
| `Checkbox` | `value: Bool = false`, `onChange: Handler = fn() {}`, `label: Option[String] = None`, `enabled: Bool = true` | Checkable option |
| `Slider` | `value: Float = 0.0`, `onChange: Handler = fn() {}`, `min: Float = 0.0`, `max: Float = 1.0`, `step: Float = 0.0`, `enabled: Bool = true` | Range selector |
| `Picker` | `value: Int = 0`, `onChange: Handler = fn() {}`, `items: List[String] = []`, `enabled: Bool = true` | Selection from items |

## Text input

| Component | Props | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TextInput` | `text: String = ""`, `onChangeText: Handler`, `placeholder: Option[String] = None`, `enabled: Bool = true`, `secureTextEntry: Bool = false` | Controlled text field; `text: $signal` binds both ways |
| `TextArea` | `value: String = ""`, `onChange: Handler = fn() {}`, `placeholder: Option[String] = None`, `maxLines: Option[Int] = None`, `enabled: Bool = true` | Multi-line input |

`TextInput` is declared in `stdlib/text_field.flux`; its public name mirrors
React Native per the public-surface naming decision (ADR-0053).

## Navigation

| Component | Props | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Router` | `initialRouteName: String = "home"` | Navigation container; shows the active `Screen` |
| `Screen` | `route: String` | A routed screen; the prop name is part of the adapter contract |

See the [navigation guide](/guides/navigation/) for the working pattern.

## Overlays

| Component | Props | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Sheet` | `onDismiss: Handler = fn() {}` | Bottom sheet |
| `Modal` | `onDismiss: Handler = fn() {}` | Modal presentation |
| `Dialog` | `onDismiss: Handler = fn() {}` | Dialog presentation |

## Motion and gesture

| Component | Props | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Animate` | `signal: Signal`, `curve: String = "easeInOut"`, `duration: Float = 0.3` | Drives a value through a curve over time |
| `Gesture` | `kind: String = "longPress"`, `onGesture: Handler = fn() {}`, `threshold: Float = 0.0` | Gesture recognizer |

## Value types and presets

| Source | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `stdlib/prelude.flux` | `Option`, `Alignment`, `Overflow`, `KeyboardType`, `ContentMode`, `Ref`, `Handler` |
| `stdlib/traits.flux` | `Numeric`, `Eq`, `Show` |
| `stdlib/color.flux` | `Color` (`RGB`) plus `red` / `green` / `blue` / `black` / `white` |
| `stdlib/font.flux` | `Font`, `Weight`, `Style` plus `body` / `title` / `caption` presets |
| `stdlib/capabilities.flux` | Capability declarations (see the [capabilities reference](/reference/capabilities/)) |
| `stdlib/platform.flux` | Platform tag and query helpers |

<Aside type="caution">Prop contracts are normative. A new prop must appear in
both the dev adapters and the release backends with the same name and type —
the adapter contract (spec Appendix F) and the parity tests enforce this, and
adding a primitive is a cross-cutting change by design.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Language reference](/reference/language/) for the syntax these
  declarations use.
- [Capabilities reference](/reference/capabilities/) for the platform
  services behind the capability declarations.


---

---
title: VM instruction set
description: The host VM's register-based ISA — signal ops, monomorphized arithmetic, list ops, closures, fault policy, and the golden vectors that pin it.
type: reference
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The host app embeds a **register-based bytecode VM**. Instructions are
monomorphized: there is no generic `ADD` with tag dispatch — there are
`ADD_I64`, `ADD_F64`, and so on. This keeps the hot path branch-free and the
execution trace byte-identical across hosts. The ISA is normative in
specification Appendix E.

## Signal operations

| Opcode | Mnemonic | Args | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `0x10` | `READ_SIGNAL` | reg_dst(u8), signal_id(u32) | Read a signal into a register |
| `0x11` | `WRITE_SIGNAL` | signal_id(u32), reg_src(u8) | Write a register's value to a signal |

A handler closure ends by writing the signals the dispatch consumed. Those
written ids, sorted ascending, become the `signals` trace event.

## Arithmetic (monomorphized)

| Opcode | Mnemonic | Args | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `0x20` | `ADD_I64` | dst, a, b (u8 each) | `dst = a + b` (i64) |
| `0x21` | `SUB_I64` | dst, a, b | `dst = a - b` |
| `0x22` | `MUL_I64` | dst, a, b | `dst = a * b` |
| `0x23` | `DIV_I64` | dst, a, b | `dst = a / b` |
| `0x24` | `MOD_I64` | dst, a, b | `dst = a % b` |

Floating-point variants (`ADD_F64`, …) occupy the same `0x2x` band with the
`F64` suffix. The counter's `count = count + 1` compiles to
`READ_SIGNAL` → `LOAD_INT_CONST` → `ADD_I64` → `WRITE_SIGNAL`.

## List operations

Four `LIST_*` opcodes back the list mutations the compiler emits for
`append` / `remove` / `clear` on `List[T]` signals. Together with the rest
of the table, the opcode vocabulary totals 61 entries (`Opcode::ALL`), and
the dev-host opcode tables are generated from that single source (see
ADR-0058) — a drifted hand-ported table fails CI before it reaches a device.

## Fault-related opcodes

| Opcode | Mnemonic | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0xD1` | `IS_NULL` | Null test used before field access; a `GET_FIELD` on `Null` faults (ADR-0024) |

## Closures and calling conventions

Handler and prop-thunk closures share the wire's `ClosureRef` encoding
(content-addressed by BLAKE3). Register conventions:

- `r0` is reserved for node context.
- `r1` holds the `ALLOC_RECORD` result on `HALT`.
- `prop_layout` maps record fields to prop indices for thunk results.

## Fault policy

| Resource | Limit | Behavior on exhaustion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas | 100,000 instructions per handler | Fault: `gas budget exhausted` |
| Memory pool | 16 MiB per frame | Fault: `memory pool exhausted` |

A thunk or handler fault leaves the node with its prior props — the render
goes stale, never blank. The error surfaces through the on-device overlay
and a trace `error` event; the view is never torn down. Division by zero
and null field access are faults too (ADR-0023, ADR-0024), not panics.

## Golden vectors

The ISA is pinned by **92 golden ISA vectors** under
[`tests/isa-vectors/`](https://github.com/elcoosp/flux/tree/main/tests/isa-vectors),
shared by the Rust oracle (`flux-vm-ref`), the shipping Swift VM
(`FluxBytecodeVM`), and the Kotlin VM. A fault-code or opcode change fails
all three implementations at once.

<Aside type="caution">Do not add opcodes without an ADR and a protocol
version bump. The dev-host opcode tables are generated from
`Opcode::ALL` — hand-editing them is the drift the parity guards exist to
catch.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [Wire protocol reference](/reference/wire-protocol/) — how closures and
  their bytecode travel to the host.
- [Testing and benchmarks](/guides/testing-and-benchmarks/) — how to run the
  vectors and the parity suite.


---

---
title: Wire protocol reference
description: The binary protocol between the dev server and host apps — frame header, patch encodings, node and value layouts, prop diffs, closures, and BLAKE3 content addressing.
type: reference
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The dev server and the host apps speak a **binary wire protocol** — the
normative Appendix D of the specification. All multi-byte integers are
little-endian. This page is a working map of the layout; the appendix in
`docs/spec/mlp-appendices.md` remains the normative source.

## Protocol version

The current protocol version is **3** (`0x03`), introduced by ADR-0059:
frame-level, node-level, and prop-level length prefixes for user-authored
collections (patches, props, children, handlers, reorder keys, and the
frame deltas) are written as **u32** instead of u16, so a 70,000-element
list prop or a >64 KB string ships to the host. A host that receives a
version it does not support rejects the handshake (`unsupported_version`).

## Frame structure

Every frame starts with a header:

| Offset | Size | Field | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 4 | magic | `0x465C5558` (`"FLUX"`) |
| 4 | 1 | version | Protocol version (currently 3) |
| 5 | 4 | seq | Monotonic sequence number |
| 9 | 1 | flags | See flag bits below |
| 10 | 2 | patch_count | Number of Patch entries |
| 12 | 2 | handler_count | Number of HandlerDef entries |
| 14 | 2 | string_count | New interned strings (0 if no delta) |
| 16 | … | patches | `[Patch; patch_count]` |
| … | … | handlers | `[HandlerDef; handler_count]` |
| … | … | strings | `[StringEntry; string_count]` (if delta) |
| … | … | state_delta | StateDelta (if flag set) |
| … | … | src_map_delta | SourceMapDelta (if flag set) |

Flag bits: 0 `full_tree` · 1 `error` · 2 `heartbeat` · 3 `has_state_delta` ·
4 `has_src_map_delta` · 5 `has_string_table_delta`.

## Patch encoding

Each patch starts with a one-byte tag:

| Tag | Type | Payload |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0x01` | Replace | u32 id, Node |
| `0x02` | Update | u32 id, PropDiff |
| `0x03` | Insert | u32 parent_id, u16 index, Node |
| `0x04` | Remove | u32 id |
| `0x05` | Reorder | u32 parent_id, key_count, `[u32; key_count]` |
| `0x06` | Handler | u32 id, ClosureRef |

The dev server computes the dirty set from written signals and emits
**Update** patches addressed only to dirty nodes, plus structural patches
where control props changed.

## Node encoding

| Field | Size | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| id | 4 | NodeId |
| kind | 1 | NodeKind (0 = Component, 1 = Primitive, …) |
| component_id | 4 | Interned component name ID |
| prop_count + props | … | `[(u16 prop_idx, Value); prop_count]` |
| child_count + children | … | `[Child; child_count]` |
| handler_count + handlers | … | `[u32 HandlerId; handler_count]` |
| span_file / span_start / span_end | 12 | Source span (FileId, byte offsets) |

## Value encoding

| Tag | Type | Payload (after tag) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0x00` | Null | (none) |
| `0x01` | Int | i64 (8 bytes) |
| `0x02` | Float | f64 (8 bytes) |
| `0x03` | Bool | u8 (0 or 1) |
| `0x04` | Str | u32 string_id (interned) |
| `0x05` | HandlerRef | u32 handler_id |
| `0x06` | List | count, `[Value; count]` |
| `0x07` | Record | count, `[(u16 prop_idx, Value); count]` |

## PropDiff encoding

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| change_count + changes | `[(u16 prop_idx, Value); change_count]` |
| removal_count + removals | `[u16 prop_idx; removal_count]` |

## Closures (ClosureRef)

Handler and prop-thunk closures share the `ClosureRef` encoding: an 8-byte
BLAKE3 hash (content address), a bytecode offset/length into the shared
blob, the captured signal ids, and a source span. On `HALT`, `r0` is
reserved for node context and `r1` holds the `ALLOC_RECORD` result; the
prop layout maps record fields to prop indices.

## Content addressing

Props, closures, and nodes are content-addressed by BLAKE3 hash. For each
item in a frame: if the hash is already in the host cache, the frame sends
only the 8-byte hash; otherwise it sends the full data and the host caches
it. After the initial `Init`, more than 90% of items are cache hits — which
is why a handler-body edit is typically a few hundred bytes on the wire.

## Handshake and pairing

Hosts authenticate during the `Hello` handshake when the server runs with
`--token`: the host presents the token read from `FLUX_DEV_TOKEN` or
`[dev] token` in `flux.toml`, and a rejected host receives no frames (see
ADR-0038 for the transport gap this closed).

<Aside type="caution">Do not add opcodes, patch tags, or frame fields
without an ADR and a protocol version bump — hosts and servers validate
against the same tables, and drift ships silent on-device faults.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [The VM instruction set](/reference/vm-isa/) — the bytecode the closures
  reference.
- [The wire, explained](/explanation/the-wire/) — why the protocol is binary
  and how patches stay tiny.


---

---
title: Build the todo app
description: Recreate the real examples/todo app step by step — records, List state, keyed ForEach, controlled text input, routing, and a Storage capability call.
type: tutorial
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This tutorial rebuilds the todo app that ships at
[`examples/todo/`](https://github.com/elcoosp/flux/tree/main/examples/todo).
Along the way you use records, list state, keyed iteration, a controlled text
input, two routed screens, and a capability call. You need a working setup
from the [first-app tutorial](/tutorials/your-first-app/) — the CLI built and
one host app runnable.

## 1. Create the project and data model

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux init todo
cd todo`} />

Replace the contents of `main.flux` with the data model: a `record` type and
a row component that renders one task.

<Code lang="rust" code={`record Task { label: String, done: Bool, }

compo TaskRow(task: Task, tasks: List[Task])
    Row gap: 8.0
        Text text: task.label
        Button text: "Remove", onPress: || { tasks.remove(task) }`} />

A `record` declares a data type with named fields. `TaskRow` shows the two
ways components receive data: the task it renders comes in as a prop, and the
owning list arrives as a second prop so the Remove handler can mutate it.

## 2. Declare the app state

Add the root component. Its `state` declarations create signals — the
reactive cells that the whole UI reads from.

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo TodoApp
    state tasks: List[Task] = [
        Task(label: "Buy milk", done: false),
        Task(label: "Walk dog", done: false),
    ]
    state newTask: String = ""`} />

- `tasks` holds the list model. The initial value is a list of record
  literals.
- `newTask` backs the text input. Assigning it in a handler updates every
  node that reads it — nothing else re-renders.

## 3. Lay out the first screen with routing

Wrap the UI in `Router` / `Screen`. The host shows only the screen whose
`route` prop matches the active route.

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo TodoApp
    // ...state declarations from step 2...

    Router initialRouteName: "tasks"
        Screen route: "tasks"
            Column gap: 12.0
                Text text: "Flux To-Do"
                Row gap: 8.0
                    TextInput text: $newTask,
                        onChangeText: fn(v) { newTask = v },
                        placeholder: "What needs doing?"
                    Button text: "Add", onPress: || {
                        tasks.append(Task(label: newTask, done: false))
                        newTask = ""
                    }`} />

Three details matter:

- **`TextInput` is controlled.** `text: $newTask` two-way binds the field to
  the signal, and `onChangeText` writes the typed value back. You reset the
  field by assigning `newTask = ""` in the Add handler.
- **List mutation is ordinary assignment.** `tasks.append(...)` is the whole
  update — there is no separate `setState`.
- **A view call owns an indented child block only when it carries at least
  one named prop.** `Router initialRouteName: "tasks"` declares `initialRouteName`,
  so its `Screen` children indent beneath it.

## 4. Render the list with a keyed ForEach

Below the input row, iterate over the tasks:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo TodoApp
    // ...state, Router, tasks screen from steps 2-3...

    Column gap: 8.0
        ForEach(tasks, key: fn(t) { t.label }) {
                        item => TaskRow(task: item, tasks: tasks)
                    }`} />

The `key` function identifies each item across edits, so the reconciler
reorders and patches existing rows in place — it does not rebuild the list
on every change. Because `TaskRow` receives `tasks` too, its Remove handler
can call `tasks.remove(task)` and the keyed diff removes exactly that row.

## 5. Reset through a capability

Add a Reset button that clears the list and the persisted copy:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo TodoApp
    // ...tasks screen from steps 2-4...

    Button text: "Reset", onPress: || {
        tasks.clear()
        Storage.removeItem(key: "todos")
    }`} />

`Storage` is a **capability** — a platform service declared in the stdlib and
resolved identically on the server and on both hosts. `Storage.removeItem`
(capability 2, method 3) reaches the host, and if the OS permission behind it
is denied, the call reports an error instead of crashing.

## 6. Add the second screen

Finish with the About screen and its navigation handlers:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo TodoApp
    // ...tasks screen from steps 2-5...
    Button text: "About", onPress: || { RouterNav.navigate("about") }

    // Second screen:

    Screen route: "about"
        Column gap: 12.0
            Text text: "About"
            Text text: "A real Flux app"
            Button text: "Back",
                onPress: || { RouterNav.navigate("tasks") }`} />

`RouterNav.navigate("about")` drives the visible screen. The `route` prop
name is part of the adapter contract — the host reads it by its hashed name,
so it must be exactly `route`.

## 7. Run it

Start the dev server from the project directory and open the host app:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux dev                 # WebSocket on :7331`} />

Point the iOS or Android host at `ws://127.0.0.1:7331` (see
[run the host app](/tutorials/your-first-app/#4-run-the-host-app) if you need
the platform steps). Add tasks, remove one, switch to the About screen and
back, then press Reset.

## 8. Ship the release forms

Generate the native sources for both platforms:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux build ios       # -> platforms/ios/Generated/main.swift
flux build android   # -> platforms/android/Generated/main.kt`} />

The generated SwiftUI and Compose code renders the same screens you ran
in dev — the parity harness proves the two paths stay equivalent.

<Aside type="note">The full source of this app lives at
`examples/todo/main.flux` in the repository, together with the `counter` and
`router` examples. Each example doubles as an integration test in CI.</Aside>

## Next steps

- [State management](/guides/state-management/) — patterns for derived values
  and shared stores.
- [Navigation](/guides/navigation/) — Router, Screen, and RouterNav in depth.
- [Capabilities](/guides/capabilities/) — the full capability surface and
  permission handling.


---

---
title: Your first Flux app
description: Build the Flux CLI, scaffold a project, hot-reload a counter on an iOS or Android host app, and ship a native release — end to end.
type: tutorial
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This tutorial walks you from a clean machine to a live, hot-reloading Flux UI
on a real device or simulator, and finishes with a native release build. It
takes about ten minutes.

## Prerequisites

| Tool | Why you need it | Check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust (rustup) | Builds the `flux` CLI | `cargo --version` |
| Xcode 16+ and XcodeGen | Runs the iOS host app (iOS 16+ target) | `xcodegen version` |
| Android Studio + JDK 17+ | Runs the Android host app | `./gradlew --version` |

You need Xcode or the Android SDK only for the host apps. Everything on the
Rust side — dev server, parser, differ, VM oracle, codegen — builds and runs
without them.

## 1. Build the CLI

From the repository root:

<Code lang="bash" code={`git clone https://github.com/elcoosp/flux
cd flux
cargo build --bin flux`} />

This produces `target/debug/flux`. Use `cargo build --release --bin flux` for
a faster binary when you plan to keep the CLI installed.

The first build provisions the pinned nightly toolchain automatically through
`rust-toolchain.toml`, so you do not select a toolchain by hand.

## 2. Scaffold a project

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux init myapp
cd myapp`} />

`flux init` writes three files into `myapp/`:

<Code lang="text" code={`myapp/
├── main.flux      # entry component: a stateful counter
├── flux.toml      # project config: name, entry, dev ports
└── .fluxignore    # build output and VCS noise`} />

Open `main.flux`. It contains the canonical Flux counter:

<Code lang="rust" code={`compo Counter
    $count: Int = 0

    Column gap: 8.0
        Text text: "tapped {count} times"
        Button text: "Increment", onPress: || { count = count + 1 }`} />

## 3. Start the dev server

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux dev`} />

You will see:

<Code lang="text" code={`Listening on ws://127.0.0.1:7331`} />

The dev server parses and type-checks every `.flux` file, lowers the program
to the Reactive Tree IR, and binds two ports:

- **WebSocket `:7331`** — the patch channel to the host apps.
- **HTTP `:7332`** — the asset server, with a `/health` probe.

Verify the server is up in another shell:

<Code lang="bash" code={`curl http://127.0.0.1:7332/health`} />

<Code lang="text" code={`ok`} />

## 4. Run the host app

The host app is precompiled native code that connects to the dev server and
renders the IR it receives. Pick your platform.

<Steps>

1. **iOS.** The host project is generated with XcodeGen:

    <Code lang="bash" code={`# from the repository root
xcodegen generate            # writes runtimes/ios/FluxApp.xcworkspace
open runtimes/ios/FluxApp.xcworkspace`} />

    Pick a simulator or a tethered device in Xcode and press **Run**. The app
    connects to `ws://127.0.0.1:7331` and renders your `Counter`.

2. **Android.** Build and install the host on a connected emulator or device:

    <Code lang="bash" code={`# from the repository root
./gradlew :runtimes:android:app:installDebug`} />

    Launch **Flux** from the launcher. It connects to `ws://127.0.0.1:7331`
    and renders the same UI.

</Steps>

Tap **Increment** in the running app. The label updates — and the next step
shows that you never recompile to change it.

## 5. Edit and watch it hot-reload

Open `main.flux` and change the `Text` label:

<Code lang="rust" code={`Text text: "tapped {count} times — wow"`} />

Save the file. The dev server diffs the tree and ships a binary patch over
the WebSocket, and the host updates in place. You never leave the running
app, and you never rebuild the host.

A handler-body edit is typically a few hundred bytes on the wire, because
props and closures are content-addressed with BLAKE3 and cached on the host
after the first `Init` frame.

## 6. Build a native release

When you want real SwiftUI or Jetpack Compose instead of the dev patch path:

<Code lang="bash" code={`flux build ios       # -> platforms/ios/Generated/main.swift
flux build android   # -> platforms/android/Generated/main.kt`} />

`flux build` lowers your `.flux` to idiomatic native source with no VM. If
`xcodebuild` or `gradle` is present on your machine, it suggests the next
build step; otherwise it emits the generated sources for you to compile.

## What you learned

- `flux init` scaffolds a project; `flux dev` serves it on `:7331`/`:7332`.
- The host apps render and hot-reload over the WebSocket patch channel.
- `flux build ios|android` emits SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose from the same
  IR — dev and release are one program, verified by the parity harness.

<Aside type="tip">Physical devices cannot reach `127.0.0.1`. See the
[dev server guide](/guides/dev-server/) for LAN exposure and pairing
tokens.</Aside>

## Next steps

Build the todo app from scratch to practice lists, routing, and capabilities:

<LinkCard title="Build the todo app" href="/tutorials/todo-app/" description="A guided tutorial through the real examples/todo app: records, lists, routing, and capabilities." />
